ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Within-subjects impossible for learning manipulation; df in ANOVA tables inconsistent
ground_truth.original_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single between-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.description: Changed between-subjects to within-subjects — impossible for this intervention (learning about IVE permanently changes cognition); df in ANOVA tables are inconsistent with within-subjects

matched_finding.subcategory: design labeled within-subjects but executed and analyzed as between-subjects
matched_finding.description: The design section explicitly states 'within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables,' but all evidence indicates a between-subjects design. Table 7 shows different participant counts per cell (159, 175, 166, 175, 159, 166) summing to N=1000, meaning each participant contributed to only one cell. The residual df in Table 9 is 994 = 1000-6, consistent only with between-subjects (N minus number of cells). In a true within-subjects design, each participant would complete all six conditions, yielding far smaller residual df. This mislabeling reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of experimental design and potentially compromises the entire analytical strategy.
matched_finding.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Self-selection into conditions visible but subtle — 'selected their preferred' reads naturally
ground_truth.original_snippet: Participants will be assigned randomly to the intervention and identifiability conditions.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

matched_finding.subcategory: self-selection into conditions instead of random assignment
matched_finding.description: The procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' Self-selection completely destroys the logic of experimental design. If participants choose their own condition, systematic differences between participants in different conditions (e.g., those who prefer to learn about the identifiable victim effect vs. those who do not) confound the treatment variable. This eliminates any basis for causal inference about the effect of intervention or identifiability on donation. The original studies used random assignment, making this a fatal deviation for a study claiming to test causal effects.
matched_finding.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Statistical victims donate MORE contradicts the identifiable victim effect being replicated
ground_truth.original_snippet: meaning that participants who faced an identifiable victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).
ground_truth.description: Reversed which condition has higher donations — IVE is now reversed (statistical > identifiable), contradicting the phenomenon being replicated and Table 11 descriptives

matched_finding.subcategory: results text reverses group means relative to data table
matched_finding.description: The results narrative states that 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' However, Table 7 shows that the identifiable victim condition has higher means in both intervention (2.58) and no-intervention (2.50) rows than the statistical victim condition (2.46 and 2.01 respectively). Weighted by cell sizes from Table 7: identifiable mean ≈ (159×2.58+175×2.50)/334 ≈ 2.54, statistical mean ≈ (175×2.46+159×2.01)/334 ≈ 2.25. The text assigns M=2.54 to statistical victims and M=2.24 to identifiable victims—exactly the reverse of what the table shows. The group labels and means are swapped.
matched_finding.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

matched_finding.subcategory: exclusion criteria stated but not applied or reported for the simulated sample
matched_finding.description: The manuscript states that 'participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.' However, no exclusion figures are reported for the simulated sample of N=1000. It is unclear how many of the 1000 generated responses were excluded and why, what the attention check consists of, how 'prior knowledge' is operationalized and measured, or what the final analytic sample is after exclusions. The Qualtrics random data generator would not implement meaningful exclusion criteria, and the reported N=1000 likely reflects pre-exclusion counts. For a real study, these details are essential for evaluating sample integrity.
matched_finding.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Availability vs affect heuristic — must know these are different mechanisms with different predictions
ground_truth.original_snippet: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The automatic "affect heuristic"  (Slovic, Finucane, Peters, & MacGregor, 2007), which relies on emotional arousal for decision making, is believed to be activa...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The "availability heuristic"  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated whe...
ground_truth.description: Replaced affect heuristic (emotional arousal) with availability heuristic (memory retrieval) — changes the theoretical mechanism; intervention design and feeling measures no longer match the theory

matched_finding.subcategory: availability heuristic misattributed as mechanism for identifiable victim effect
matched_finding.description: The manuscript states that the 'availability heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual.' The availability heuristic concerns frequency and probability judgments based on ease of recall — it is not the accepted mechanism for the identifiable victim effect. The correct mechanism, as established by Small & Loewenstein (2003) cited in the same paragraph and explicitly central to the target article being replicated, is the affect heuristic: emotional/affective responses to identifiable victims drive prosocial motivation. Slovic et al. (2007) — a paper cited in the references — specifically distinguishes affective processing from availability. This is a fundamental theoretical error that mischaracterizes the core mechanism the replication claims to study.
matched_finding.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003).

matched_finding.subcategory: exploratory analyses not distinguished from confirmatory pre-registered tests
matched_finding.description: The manuscript lists numerous analyses in Table 5 (pairwise comparisons, post-hoc contrasts, correlations across six conditions, segregated feeling ANOVAs) but does not clearly distinguish which are pre-registered confirmatory tests versus exploratory follow-ups. The OSF pre-registration link is provided but the specific pre-registered hypotheses are not reproduced in the manuscript. The addition of the joint/no intervention and joint/intervention conditions to the original contrast test represents a major analytical expansion. The extension hypothesis (H6) uses the same dataset with no power analysis specifically for this extension. Without transparent delineation of confirmatory vs. exploratory analyses, familywise error control cannot be evaluated.
matched_finding.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period. Power analyses and all materials used in these experiments are available in the supplementary materials.
